title: Killing the ivory tower - how Jumbo rebuilt architecture around teams
summary: What happens when you stop gatekeeping architecture and hand it to the people building the system. 🧊
body_markdown:
Microservices were supposed to make change easier. For a lot of companies, they did the opposite: services multiply, teams drift into silos, and every change cuts across a myriad of teams.


In a recent episode of the **Dear Architects** podcast, Luca spoke with Onur, a staff engineer and tech lead at Jumbo, about how they dealt with exactly that. His view is that the ‘ivory tower’ is dead, and that every engineer now needs to think like an architect.


## 🛒 Meet Jumbo


Jumbo is the second-largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands and a 100-year-old business. When Onur joined, it ran two big monoliths. Like everyone else, Jumbo moved to microservices. Engineering grew from around 20 people to more than 350, new services appeared every week, and the monoliths were quickly strangled. The result was a very complex architecture where change wasn’t easy.


## 🔍 Five promotion services and nobody talking


One of the first things Onur’s team did was run a big picture event storming session on the order flow, with business and engineering teams in the room.


They found five different promotion microservices, built by teams who didn’t know the others existed. It was Conway’s law at work. Siloed teams had produced a siloed architecture.


## 🧩 A simpler core domain chart


Next came Onur’s favourite exercise, a simplified version of Nick Tune’s core domain chart:


1. The team writes down everything that adds cognitive load (infrastructure, features, services, support work) on sticky notes.
2. They cluster the notes together. This is where different perspectives show up, sometimes as people using different words for the same thing, like “article” versus “product.”
3. They capture pain points and proposals.
4. They plot everything across the **generic** , **supporting** and **core** layers.


The proposals then become C4 models or ADRs, depending on whether other teams are affected.


With the loyalty team, the exercise turned up more than 20 microservices for a team of 7. Many were small services built because no single source of truth for customers or stores existed at the time. Once one did, they could be consolidated. Six to eight months later, the team was down to around 10.


## 🗺️ Diagrams with intention


Jumbo models its architecture with the C4 model in IcePanel. Context diagrams barely change, so they age well. Most of the technical views live at **Level 2 (Container)** , where you can see how applications interact and who owns what. They skip code-level diagrams entirely, because the code changes too fast.


They also don’t try to capture everything. Diagrams are built around specific scenarios, like the order flow, with everything else abstracted away.


Those scenarios are also linked to incident management. When Jumbo’s 24/7 on-call team gets an alert about search, they might not recognise a service that’s named after its technology. They can find the search scenario diagram, though, and see straight away which services are probably involved. Because the diagrams get used when production is on fire, teams have a real reason to keep them current. ADRs are linked to them too.


## 🔼 Bottom up, not top down


Many teams were originally organised around technology, with names like “the SAP team” or “the integration team.” Moving to **Team Topologies** and stream-aligned teams was a long journey, and Onur chose to do it bottom up. Top-down decisions tend to play out like the telephone game, where the message gets lost on the way down.


The approach looked like this:


- **Listen first.** They sat down one-on-one with key stakeholders and most senior developers and asked what was dragging them down. They repeat this every quarter. The biggest pain point was too many hops between teams to deliver any value.
- **Build a shared language.** Chapters and guilds made sure everyone understood concepts like stream-aligned, enabling and complicated-subsystem teams.
- **Then go to the C-suite** for buy-in, and pilot a few subdomains with the business as success stories.


It didn’t go perfectly. Early on, Onur wanted every team on board. Then the SAP teams pushed back. SAP is a whole ecosystem, and its natural structure doesn’t always fit stream-aligned teams. Instead of forcing it, they found a sweet spot. As Luca pointed out, generic and supporting domains change at a different rate, so it’s fine to treat them differently.


## 🏛️ Architecture without the ivory tower


At Jumbo, senior engineers already switch between implementation, staff engineer and architect roles day to day. AI makes this more pressing. When code is quick to write, the bottleneck becomes putting changes in the right place so you don’t end up with a big ball of mud. That can’t depend on a few gatekeeping architects. It has to sit with the teams, through collaborative modelling.


For changes that cut across several domains, Jumbo uses two mechanisms:


- A **technical leadership group** of staff engineers and architects that meets biweekly.
- **Working groups** : temporary, time-boxed teams of 6 to 8 weeks, pulled from several streams. When a government regulation landed that touched multiple domains, a working group delivered it without restructuring any stream-aligned teams.


## 🤖 A rubber duck in the pipeline


Onur’s rule for AI is to try things in your own work first, and only roll them out once you’ve found the value. A recent agentic engineering workshop went well enough that teams are now asking for more sessions. Participants left with their own agent pipeline:


1. An **analyst agent** reads the assigned Jira ticket via MCP and drafts requirements and an action plan.
2. A **rubber duck agent** , acting like a smart senior colleague, challenges the plan and its trade-offs.
3. An **architect agent** checks the plan against existing ADRs.
4. An **implementer agent** writes and tests the code, using skills that encode Jumbo’s API guidelines and conventions.


Those skills are what make the difference. Juniors worried about being replaced and seniors thought the output was poor. Now juniors feel more senior because their plans get challenged before the PR, and seniors came round once a central skills repository covered Jumbo’s own front-end framework and design system.


Onur is just as clear that you don’t need AI for everything. The first question is whether it can be done without it, and more than half the time it can. Jumbo moves slowest with AI in customer-facing systems, faster in internal tools, and fastest in developer experience, where the output is still deterministic code.


## 🏁 Conclusion


Onur’s advice for anyone starting a similar transformation comes down to three things. Pick your battles: 70% adoption might be your sweet spot, and this is a marathon, not a sprint. Make sure your engineering culture is ready, with champions and chapters to spread knowledge. And think about hiring, because you can’t build stream-aligned teams while hiring for a different mindset. When architecture belongs to the teams, backed by shared language, intentional diagrams and lightweight decision records, it scales better than any ivory tower.
